Taught 2 years in inner city public schools. There is a whole art and science to this subject called Classroom Management. I could write a book on it but somebody already did: Tools for Teaching by Fred Jones. The idea is to create well ordered classroom environment which makes dealing with any one non-compliant student easier. When you have 29 other students going along with the classroom order it creates a social pressure to conform. Beyond that you need a well established escalation mechanism (warning, stay after class, sent to principle, in school suspension etc.). Make it well understood, predictable, and consistent so that non-compliant students know exactly the consequence of each action. Ultimately, if you are really good at classroom management, you should rarely if ever have to deal with it. Drain the swamp properly and noncompliance won't become an issue in the first place.

Cyclist here and I've been hit about a half dozen times, ending up in the emergency room a couple times. While I'm not a lawyer, I can still give some relevant advice.

  1. the laws that come into play vary state by state

  2. in most cases, the person driving the motor vehicle is responsible for reporting the accident to the police

  3. there are only a handful of states that have a contributory negligence law (i.e. you pay a certain percentage of the costs based on how much at fault you are). IIRC, it's Maryland, Virginia, and DC, so as long as you weren't hit in any of those states, you shouldn't worry much, which brings me to...

  4. You tell that collections agency they can go suck a dick. Let me tell you something. Collections agencies are terrible. They will try to extort money from you, even if you're not legally required to pay it. They can tell you that you're liable for the damages all they want. Until they send a collection notice, ignore them and tell them to stop calling you. If they do send a notice, dispute it. Most states have some sort of no-fault law, making the lady's insurance responsible for covering not only the damages to her vehicle, but your medical bills as well.

Again, I'm not a lawyer, but I've gone through this hell personally and ended up having to become familiar with the legalese on this topic to fend off the insurance companies and collection agencies and get them to fight amongst each other instead of me. My credit is still intact and I have had to pay zero dollars from my accidents (unless you include the money I dropped for one of those online fax services so I can send paperwork with ease since both types of companies refuse to accept it via email).

If you PM me with the state that you were hit in, I can look up the local laws and try to give you more specific information and advice. In the future, call the police. You can refuse medical treatment if you're worried about debt, but you always always always want that police report.
